arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Elwood argued that aiding and abetting requires purposeful intent to facilitate the crime.
Mr. Elwood stated that mere knowing assistance is insufficient for liability.
Justice Scalia questioned if knowing a crime involves firearms is enough for liability.
Justice Alito asked if the aider learns about the gun after the crime happens.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the mental state required for accomplice liability. the side that brought the case argues that knowing a gun is present is not enough. The government argues that knowing a gun is present satisfies the legal standard.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the conviction overturned because the jury did not find intent to facilitate gun use.
The government wants the conviction to stand because the side that brought the case knew a gun was present during the crime.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the mental state needed for accomplice liability. It determines when a helper faces charges for a crime involving a weapon. The outcome shapes how prosecutors prove intent in joint criminal activities.
